            Austin C. and Janet L. Rose are ranchers in Burnet County, living on a historic and

culturally significant ranch that has been in the Taylor family for six generations (the

“Taylor-Rose Ranch”).             The Texas Historical Commission (“THC”) has included the

entire Taylor-Rose Ranch in its database of archeologically and culturally significant

properties, assigning it Trinomial No. 41BT562.1            The ranch is located along Link G6,

which not only bisects the historic working ranch but also comes within 375 feet of the

Roses’s home.             The Roses, in their individual capacities and as trustees of the Joppa

1886 Trust, file their response to exceptions filed by Save the Lampasas (and related

parties), Cherokee Creek Partners (and related parties), the Sneeds, and applicants Oncor

Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation

(“Applicants”).

I.         As the ALJs correctly found, Applicants did not prove that the proposed 765-
           kV line is necessary.

           The ALJs correctly analyzed the issues with the development of Permian Basin

Reliability Plan and the effect of changed circumstances since the PBRP was approved.

It is Applicants, not the ALJs, that are inconsistent: Applicants discount announced power

generation projects in West Texas as speculative, while it asks that the PUC treat

announced speculative grid requirements totaled two years ago (including those based on

2022 surveys of energy companies) as solid.2              Also, to the extent these generation

projects were announced after the Permian Basin Reliability Plan was adopted, and

ERCOT is the only entity that can evaluate the probability that generation would be built,

 the solution is to require ERCOT to reevaluate based on current conditions, before

irrevocably taking private property and expending billions for which the public will be on

the hook.3      Finally, importantly, Applicants fail to identify new sources of generation in

the area in which Import Path 2 would be built, from East Bell County East to Big Hill.

Instead, we know that Central Texas itself needs to import electricity.4                         Applicants—

who get a guaranteed rate of return on their investments, poor or not—did not prove that

Import Path 2 is necessary.                 Taking Texans’ property to subsidize speculative

cryptocurrency mines and data centers is un-American and un-Texan.                          The Commission

should deny the Application because Applicants have not proven a need for Import Path 2.

II.     Should the PUC grant the Application, Save the Lampasas’ preferred Route
        296 is not only inferior to Routes 894 or 487—it is not viable.

        Should the PUC grant the Application, Save the Lampasas’ preferred route, Route

296, is not only inferior to Routes 894 and 487, it is not viable.5                    Among its problems

are the following:

             • Route 296 uses Link G6, which includes the historically significant Taylor-

                 Rose Ranch—the entirety of which is in a trinomial by the Texas Historical

                 Commission, and which contains other historical and archeologically

                 significant properties.

              • Route 296 uses Link J31, which would interfere with the cathodic

              • Route 296 uses Link F34, which includes the Florence ISD elementary

                  compressor station on two sides.

         A.       Link G6 contains the Taylor-Rose Ranch, the entirety of which is
                  within the boundaries of the trinomial issued by the Texas Historical
                  Commission—and its 7,224 foot length cannot be spanned.

         Save the Lampasas states that a historic heritage ranch need not be completely

avoided but that siting professional will seek to suggest a route that avoids significant

features of the site’s trinomial.7          It cites Cherokee Creek’s witness, Ms. Reinecke, for the

proposition that eligible trinomials can be crossed by development if it would not be

detrimental to the eligibility of that trinomial.8 But Reinecke testified only about the

true in general, there is a difference between a property that may have a trinomial-eligible

resource that is located somewhere within its property lines, on one hand, and a

property—such as the Taylor-Rose Ranch—that is completely within the boundaries of a

trinomial, on the other.

         Certainly, in the ordinary case, a utility may be able to span over, say, a scattering

of arrowheads, or a cave, or other culturally important resource.                             Applicants testified

that if significant archeological sites are identified during the field investigation,

Applicants will work with the THC to “shift structure locations along the route alignment

to span the site, thereby avoiding the placement of foundations within recorded site

boundaries.”10         Here, the recorded site boundaries of Trinomial No. 41BT562 are the

entirety of the Taylor-Rose Ranch,11 which runs for 7,224 feet.12                           It is not possible for

Applicants to span 7,224 feet.               Applicants testified that the 765-kV steel lattice tower

that will primarily be used for the Proposed Transmission Line Project “generally allows

for a typical span length of approximately 1,400–1,500 feet.”13                        Applicants’ witness, Ms.

Cooley, further testified that, “The maximum span that we anticipate would probably be

        B.       Link G6 bifurcates numerous other properties that are also historically
                 important, generational ranches, and would cross riparian lands,
                 wetlands, and streams.

        Link G6 is defined by the North Fork of the San Gabriel River and its named

tributaries (Allen Branch, Campbell’s Creek, and Olive Branch), working ranches, and

family homesteads.15          The entire 16.16-mile length of Link G6 contains generational

ranches and other properties that would also be bisected by Route 296.                         Unsurprisingly,

given the historic Taylor-Rose Ranch, Link G6 (part of Route 296), has 25,179 feet of

high archeological/historical site potential, compared to only 3,810 on Link G52 and

8,277 on Link G51 (parts of Route 894).16

        The G6 Landowners Legal Fund, LLC (“G6 landowners”), and eleven of its

members, presented extensive evidence of the residential, agricultural, recreational, and

conservation use of properties along Link G6.17                 Link G6 does not parallel any existing

        D.       Link J31 would interfere with cathodic protection, would fragment

        The use of Link J31 is also a problem.                     The possibility of interfering with

cathodic protection is real, which is why the PUC changed its rule regarding the

paralleling of pipelines.        Call it prudent location: why would one possibly degrade crude

oil, natural gas, and highly volatile liquids pipelines, as those pipelines traverse the

Colorado River?26          Additionally, the Colorado River Alliance Intervenors27 testified

extensively that the use of Link J31 would result in the fragmentation of dedicated

golden-cheeked warbler habitat. Finally, as other intervenors have noted, Link J31,

unlike other proposed crossings, roughly parallels the Colorado River for about 2 miles

transmission line could be moved to avoid the 500-child elementary school that now

exists on Link F34, in Florence Independent School District.30                     But the map shows little

room to maneuver, without moving too close to adjoining properties that did not receive

notice.        More importantly, the Florence Independent School District, which believes the

school will grow to 740 students, does not think that is a possibility.31                        Also, PUC

witness Mr. Poole testified on cross-examination that the presence of the elementary

school was an issue and other routes should be explored.32

          F.       Link G31 crosses an existing 42-inch natural gas pipeline, will cross
                   and closely parallel an in-development 48-inch natural gas pipeline,
                   and also parallels a compressor station on two sides.

          That Route 296 utilizes Link G31 is also problematic.                   Link G31 is the site of the

Florence Compressor Station, which supports the 42-inch natural gas pipeline Matterhorn

Express Pipeline.33           Additionally, a 450-mile, 48-inch natural gas pipeline—the Eiger

Express Pipeline—has been planned and will be in service no later than mid-2028.34

The 48-inch Eiger Express Pipeline will follow the same easement as the 42-inch natural

gas pipeline.35        Route 296 crosses the 42-inch Matterhorn Express Pipeline twice, close

          G.      Route 296—unlike Routes 894 or 487—parallels streams within 100

          Save the Lampasas has repeatedly invoked the decision in PUC Docket No. 37463

to insist that Route 894 should not be selected.37                 But in Docket No. 37463, the line that

this case, Save the Lampasas’s chosen Route 296 parallels streams within 100 feet, for

686 feet of its length, while Routes 894 and 487 do not parallel any stream within 100

feet.39    Using Save the Lampasas’s own arguments, Route 296 should not be chosen.

        H.      Conclusion: Route 296 is inferior to Routes 894 and 487.

       For all of these reasons, Route 296 is inferior to Routes 894 and 487:

            • Link G6, which includes the Taylor-Rose Ranch as well as other historic

               properties that would be bisected by Route 296, is undevelopable.

            • Links I1 and J6 also contain historically and archeologically important

               properties, including mutigenerational ranches.

            • Link J31 would interfere with cathodic protection on the existing natural gas

               pipeline, would fragment golden cheeked warbler habitat, and closely

               parallels the Colorado River for almost two miles.

            • Link F34 runs close to the 500-child elementary school of the Florence

               Independent School District.

            • Link G31 crosses an existing 42-inch natural gas pipeline, will also cross a

               48-inch natural gas pipeline, and parallels a compressor station on two sides.

            • Route 296 parallels stream within 100 feet, for roughly 686 feet.

III.   Should the PUC grant the Application, Cherokee Creek’s CCG route is not
       only inferior to Routes 894 and 487—it is not viable.

       A.      Cherokee Creek, espousing Route CCG, continues to misstate by 50%
               the number of recorded cultural resources that Route CCG crosses and
               wrongly concludes Route CCG performs on par with Routes 894 and
               487.

       The Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors (“Cherokee Creek”) espouse Route CCG,

which also includes Link G6.      In its exceptions, Cherokee Creek continues to wrongly

Routes 296 and 392.         Cherokee Creek states:

        Measured against the Southern-corridor Route 296 and the Northen
        corridor Route 392, the record is more lopsided still: Route CCG crosses
        only 2 recorded cultural resource sites (the same as Routes 487 and 894),
        while Route 296 crosses 4 and Route 392 crosses 16.40

Cherokee Creek’s statement that Route CCG only crosses two recorded cultural resource

sites is simply wrong: Route CCG crosses three recorded cultural resource sites, while

Routes 894 and 487 cross two.

        Although it is true that Applicants’ original EA, Table 7-3 showed no recorded

cultural resources on Link G6, evidence adduced at hearing showed that both Applicants’

original EA, and its updated Exhibit 23, failed to include the known, recorded cultural

resource on Link G6, Trinomial No. 41BT562.41                      Applicants’ witness, Mr. Marusak,

verified that information on cross-examination.42               Cherokee Creek’s counsel was present

for the hearing, which included the Roses’ several cross-examinations regarding

Trinomial No. 41BT562 and even the Roses’s cross-examination of Cherokee Creek’s

expert witness, Ms. Reinecke.43

        When Trinomial No. 41BT562 is included, Route CCG, Route 894 and Route 487

are not identical, since neither Route 894 nor Route 487 use Link G6 but Route CCG

does.    Instead, Route 894 and Route 487 each cross two recorded cultural resources sites,

and Route CCG crosses three, one being the entire 7,224 feet across the Taylor-Rose
